brand.name: flite-rs
brand.eyebrow: Carnegie Mellon lineage, rewritten in Rust
brand.standfirst: A speech synthesiser small enough to live inside a web page.
brand.note: Nothing you type leaves this machine. The voice is compiled into the page.
brand.footer: flite-rs is Apache-2.0. The voices come from CMU and keep their own terms.

engines.label: Clustergen
engines.note: Statistical parametric. No recordings: mel-cepstral trajectories predicted by regression trees, run through an MLSA filter. Voice cmu_us_slt, 16 kHz.

engines.label: Diphone 16k
engines.note: Concatenative. Recorded diphones spliced together and resynthesised at the pitch the model asks for. Voice cmu_us_kal, 16 kHz.

engines.label: Diphone 8k
engines.note: The same technique on the 8 kHz database — the one upstream Flite ships by default, and the smallest download here.

samples.label: Long
samples.text: Speech synthesis by rule has a long history at Carnegie Mellon. Festival came first, then Flite, which stripped the same models down until they fit on a handheld. This is that engine again, written from the published descriptions rather than translated from the source, and compiled to run where you are reading.

about.body:
flite-rs is a clean-room Rust implementation of the synthesis techniques behind CMU's Flite and Festival: CART models for phrasing, duration and intonation, rule-based letter-to-sound, and two ways of turning phones into sound.

No C, no FFI, no unsafe, and no runtime dependencies. The browser build here is a plain wasm32-unknown-unknown target with a hand-written calling convention — there is no bindgen and no JavaScript toolchain anywhere in the deploy.
